Recent work supports grounding recommendation judgments in identifiable items and actual user feedback. SIGIR 2024’s [Rethinking the Evaluation of Dialogue Systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12994) finds that showing user feedback changes human and LLM assessments of relevance, usefulness, interestingness, and explanation quality. [MGFRec (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3770854.3780206) emphasizes grounding recommendation reasoning in the actual item space, although its agent-generated feedback does not establish real-user preferences.

A practical protocol synthesized from these findings: record user ID, recommendation ID, displayed rank, exact feedback span, and supporting title/description/history evidence. Annotate specific relevance separately from broad thematic similarity. Distinguish explicit mismatch, unidentified recommendation referent, and insufficient evidence; preserve abstention when identity or relevance cannot be established. Treat compatibility and ownership as unknown unless explicitly supported. Historical interaction establishes interaction, not necessarily ownership, satisfaction, or present intent. These are proposed operational rules, not a validated taxonomy from one paper.

Reliability requires independent annotation of the same examples before adjudication, reporting raw agreement, an appropriate chance-corrected statistic, label frequencies, abstention rates, and recurrent disagreements. [Sources of Disagreement (2025)](https://aclanthology.org/2025.comedi-1.3/) shows that annotation format and annotator choice change instance-level labels even when aggregate agreement appears stable. [Fröbe et al. (SIGIR 2025)](https://downloads.webis.de/publications/papers/froebe_2025e.pdf) finds LLM relevance assessors agree more with one another than with humans and overestimate LLM rerankers. Therefore, model agreement alone cannot validate inferred user intent; retain human checks and evidence-linked uncertainty.
